newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian foreign debt may reach $8 bln by 1999.
newsitem.headline: Croatian foreign debt may reach $8 bln by 1999.

text.p: Croatia's foreign debt may grow to $8 billion from current $4.8 billion by 1999, but this should not create servicing problems, central bank governor Marko Skreb said.

The bank's recent projections show that if Croatia continues to borrow abroad at its current sustainable pace, total foreign debt could reach $8 billion in the next three years, said Skreb, governor of the National Bank of Croatia.
"We make various projections, optimistic and pessimistic ones -- this is a realistic one," Skreb told Reuters in an interview this week.
"A foreign debt of $8 billion should not worry us. Both statically and dynamically, these are not figures that could in any way cause concern."
Many analysts have been warning the authorities against accumulating too much external debt, pointing to the grim experience of former federal Yugoslavia in the early 1980s.

Zagreb University economist Mate Babic said growth in Croatian foreign debt resembled that of old Yugoslavia in 1977-82, when it doubled to $20 billion, causing an acute debt crisis and economic collapse.
But Skreb said there was no alternative to foreign borrowing for Croatia at this stage.
"It is absolutely vital for Croatia, given the lack of domestic savings and the need to invest, for investment to be financed from abroad."
All data used to measure levels of indebtedness show that Croatia is "a very, very low-indebted country", he said.
Croatia current foreign debt, most of which was inherited from Yugoslavia, equals about 23 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
The debt-to-service ratio, which measures the portion of the country's total hard currency income needed to repay the arrears, is put at less than 10 percent.
"According to our projections, servicing the debt in the mid-term, till 2000, should remain under 10 percent of the foreign currency income," Skreb said.

Given that reserves of the central and commercial banks topped $4 billion in January, the net debt is under $1 billion, which is not a problem for a country with strong tourism and export-oriented industry like Croatia, said Skreb.
After four years of war and recession, the Croatian economy is recovering strongly and the government expects it to grow at a healthy rate in the next several years.
"The ratio of foreign debt to GDP will grow slightly till 2000, but so will GDP. We expect a nominal growth of GDP of some 10 percent a year, with inflation of three to four percent," Skreb said.
Memories of the Yugoslav debt crisis are still fresh in the minds of many Croats since it led to fuel shortages, power blackouts and, finally, the violent break-up of the federation.
Most critics warn that borrowing abroad must be a function of spurring faster economic growth and call for the reduction of the state sector in new debt.
